Bithiah
bith-EYE-ah
n. (proper name; a daughter of Pharaoh who married into Judah)
Hebrew Bithyah, daughter of the LORD, from bath (daughter) and the divine element -yah. For an Egyptian princess to bear such a name is itself a testimony.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

Bithiah is named once: “And these are the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, which Mered took” (1 Chronicles 4:18). A Pharaoh's daughter married a man of Judah, and her children are enrolled in the tribe of the promise. The name is the striking thing. Bithyah means daughter of the LORD, compounded with the covenant name, and an Egyptian princess did not receive such a name at birth in the house of Pharaoh. The likeliest reading — and the dictionary offers it as a reading, not a certainty — is that this was a name taken, as Ruth took the God of Israel and Rahab took her place in Jericho's wall on the side of the LORD. If so, the Chronicler has quietly recorded a conversion. The genealogy of Judah, which runs toward David and toward Christ, contains a Gentile woman out of the house that had enslaved Israel, and it names her daughter of the LORD. “And Esrom begat Aram” is how the line reads in Matthew; but the line has Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba in it, and in Chronicles it has this woman too.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Bithiah is a Hebrew proper name and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.

expand to see more

Bithiah is a Hebrew proper name; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.

The name appears once, in 1 Chronicles 4:18.

She is called the daughter of Pharaoh, and the wife of Mered of Judah.

The name means daughter of the LORD, with the divine element -yah.

Her sons are enrolled in the genealogy of Judah.

Key Scripture

1Ch 4:18 — "And his wife Jehudijah bare Jered the father of Gedor, and Heber the father of Socho, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah. And these are the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, which Mered took."

Rut 1:16 — "And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:"

Mat 1:5 — "And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth; and Obed begat Jesse;"

Isa 56:3 — "Neither let the son of the stranger, that hath joined himself to the LORD, speak, saying, The LORD hath utterly separated me from his people: neither let the eunuch say, Behold, I am a dry tree."

Modern Corruption

Israel's genealogies are read as records of ethnic purity; they repeatedly enrol Gentiles who joined themselves to the LORD.

expand to see more

The common charge is that Old Testament Israel was defined by blood and closed to outsiders. The genealogies themselves are the refutation. Judah's line holds Tamar, Rahab of Jericho, Ruth the Moabitess, and here a daughter of Pharaoh bearing a name compounded with the covenant name of God. Scripture does not hide these women; Matthew names three of them in the first chapter of the New Testament.

The principle to recover is that the covenant was always entered by faith and not by descent. “Neither let the son of the stranger, that hath joined himself to the LORD, speak, saying, The LORD hath utterly separated me from his people” (Isaiah 56:3). What Ezra later opposed was not foreign blood but foreign gods, and Bithiah is the case that proves the distinction: a foreign woman named daughter of the LORD, married into Judah, with her sons in the record.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Bithyah, daughter of the LORD; a daughter of Pharaoh married to Mered of Judah.

expand to see more

Hebrew Bithyah, from bath (daughter) and the divine element -yah.

The sense is daughter of the LORD, or daughter of Jah.

The single occurrence is 1 Chronicles 4:18.

She is identified as the daughter of Pharaoh and wife of Mered.

An Egyptian princess would not bear such a name from birth.

Usage

"the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, which Mered took"

"thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God"

"the son of the stranger, that hath joined himself to the LORD"
